incidents.title: United States judge bars the press from reporting a murder suspect's confession before trial
incidents.summary: On October 27, 1975, Nebraska District Judge Hugh Stuart ordered news organizations covering a mass murder near Sutherland, Nebraska, not to report a suspect's confession or other evidence before jury selection. The Supreme Court of the United States, the country's highest court, struck down the order on June 30, 1976, ruling that the government had not shown the heavy justification a prior restraint on publication requires.
incidents.what_happened: On the evening of October 18, 1975, local police found six members of the Kellie family murdered in their home in Sutherland, Nebraska, a town of about 850 people. Police released the description of a suspect, Erwin Charles Simants, to reporters who had gone to the scene, and Simants was arrested the next morning. The Lincoln County Attorney and Simants's own lawyer asked a county court to restrict reporting on the case, and on October 27 the District Court of Lincoln County, under Judge Hugh Stuart, replaced that order with its own, finding a clear and present danger that pretrial publicity could impinge on Simants's right to a fair trial. Stuart's order barred news organizations from reporting the existence or content of Simants's confession and other evidence until a jury was chosen. Nebraska Press Association and other news organizations appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States, the country's highest court. On June 30, 1976, the Court ruled unanimously that the heavy burden required to justify a prior restraint, an order stopping publication in advance, had not been met, and it reversed the judgment of the Nebraska Supreme Court that had upheld the order.
incidents.stated_justification: Judge Stuart found that, because of the nature of the crimes charged, there was a clear and present danger that pretrial publicity could impinge on Simants's right to a fair trial.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Stuart's order barred news organizations from reporting the existence or content of Simants's confession, the contents of a note he had written and other evidence, until a jury was chosen.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The killing of six members of one family drew widespread local, regional and national news coverage in a small Nebraska town, and courts were weighing how to balance a defendant's right to a fair trial against the press's right to report on pending criminal proceedings.
incidents.outcome_note: The Supreme Court of the United States reversed the restrictive order on June 30, 1976, finding the government had not met the heavy burden required to justify a prior restraint on publication.

incidents.title: United States police search a student newspaper's offices for photographs of a protest
incidents.jurisdiction: Palo Alto and Santa Clara County, California, United States
incidents.summary: On April 12, 1971, Palo Alto police searched the newsroom of The Stanford Daily, a student newspaper, for photographs of a clash between demonstrators and police at Stanford University Hospital, though no member of the paper's staff was suspected of a crime. The Supreme Court of the United States ruled 5 to 3 on May 31, 1978, that the search did not violate the First or Fourth Amendments.
incidents.what_happened: Late in the day on April 9, 1971, officers of the Palo Alto Police Department and the Santa Clara County Sheriff's Department responded to a call from the director of Stanford University Hospital in California asking them to remove demonstrators who had occupied the hospital's administrative offices since the previous afternoon. Nine police officers were hurt in the resulting confrontation. The next day, The Stanford Daily, a student newspaper at Stanford University, published photographs of the clash. On April 12, 1971, the Santa Clara County District Attorney's office obtained a warrant from a municipal court to search the Daily's offices for photographs and negatives that might identify people involved in the felonies of "battery on a peace officer" and "assault with a deadly weapon." Four police officers searched the newsroom's photo laboratory, filing cabinets, desks and wastebaskets that day, though the warrant did not allege that any Daily staff member had committed a crime, and the search turned up nothing beyond photographs the paper had already published. The Daily sued the police and prosecutors, arguing the search violated the First and Fourth Amendments. On May 31, 1978, the Supreme Court of the United States ruled 5 to 3 that a search warrant for a newsroom not itself suspected of a crime was constitutional.
incidents.stated_justification: The warrant was issued on a finding that photographs and film relevant to the identity of the perpetrators of felonies, "battery on a peace officer" and "assault with a deadly weapon," would be found on the Daily's premises.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The warrant affidavit did not allege that any member of the Daily's staff had committed a crime, and the search itself turned up nothing beyond the photographs the newspaper had already published.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: A confrontation between police and demonstrators occupying Stanford University Hospital's administrative offices had injured nine officers, and prosecutors wanted photographs the student newspaper had taken of the clash to identify people involved.
incidents.outcome_note: The Supreme Court of the United States ruled 5 to 3 that the search of the Daily's newsroom did not violate the First or Fourth Amendments.

incidents.title: United Kingdom court bars The Sunday Times from publishing an article on thalidomide
incidents.summary: On November 17, 1972, the Divisional Court of the Queen's Bench Division, part of England's High Court, granted the Attorney General's request for an injunction stopping The Sunday Times from publishing an article about the drug thalidomide, on the ground that it would amount to contempt of court. The European Court of Human Rights ruled on April 26, 1979, by eleven votes to nine, that the injunction breached Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the treaty provision protecting freedom of expression.
incidents.what_happened: Thalidomide, a sedative marketed in Britain in the early 1960s, caused severe birth defects in children whose mothers took it during pregnancy. Families of affected children sued the manufacturer, Distillers Company, and a settlement was still being negotiated a decade later. The Sunday Times prepared an article examining how Distillers had tested and marketed the drug. The Attorney General for England and Wales, the government's chief legal officer, applied to stop publication, arguing the article would prejudge issues still before the courts. On November 17, 1972, the Divisional Court of the Queen's Bench Division granted an injunction restraining Times Newspapers Ltd. from publishing the article on the ground that it would constitute contempt of court. The Court of Appeal discharged the injunction on February 16, 1973, but the House of Lords, then the United Kingdom's highest court, restored it in modified form after a further appeal. The injunction was discharged on June 23, 1976, and The Sunday Times published the article four days later. The newspaper's publisher brought the case to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled on April 26, 1979, by eleven votes to nine, that the injunction had breached Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.
incidents.stated_justification: The House of Lords directed that Times Newspapers Ltd. be restrained from publishing any article or matter which prejudges the issues of negligence, breach of contract or breach of duty in the pending thalidomide litigation.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The Sunday Times was barred from publishing its article on the thalidomide litigation from November 1972 until the injunction was discharged on June 23, 1976; the newspaper published the article four days later.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Thalidomide, which caused severe birth defects in children whose mothers took it during pregnancy, had drawn nationwide public and parliamentary attention in Britain, and the House of Commons extensively debated the pending compensation settlement with the manufacturer on November 29, 1972.
incidents.outcome_note: The European Court of Human Rights ruled on April 26, 1979, by eleven votes to nine, that the injunction against The Sunday Times had breached Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

incidents.title: South Africa bans The World and Weekend World newspapers and detains editor Percy Qoboza
incidents.summary: On October 19, 1977, a day South Africans came to call Black Wednesday, the government banned the newspapers The World and Weekend World and had the Special Branch police arrest editor Percy Qoboza and deputy editor Aggrey Klaaste. Qoboza was detained without charge under the Internal Security Act until his release in March 1978, and The World did not resume publication.
incidents.what_happened: Percy Qoboza had edited The World, then South Africa's most widely read Black newspaper, since 1974, and the paper had covered the 1976 Soweto uprising and its aftermath. On October 19, 1977, the Special Branch of the South African Police arrested Qoboza and Aggrey Klaaste, the news editor of the affiliated Weekend World, in an operation South African History Online describes as a mission to shut down the two Black publications. The government banned The World and Weekend World the same day and detained Qoboza under section 10 of the Internal Security Act, holding him without charge at Modderbee Prison, east of Johannesburg; Klaaste was held there as well. The same day, the government banned nineteen Black Consciousness Movement organizations and detained scores of their members, weeks after the death in police custody of Black Consciousness leader Steve Biko. Aggrey Klaaste later wrote that police came to his home in Meadowlands on the morning of the arrests to read him a detention notice. Qoboza was released in March 1978 after international pressure. The World did not reopen; Qoboza went on to edit a different newspaper, the Post.
incidents.stated_justification: The government held Qoboza and Klaaste under section 10 of the Internal Security Act, a law that let authorities detain people without charge or trial, without publicly detailing an individual reason for their detention.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The World and Weekend World stopped publishing after the ban, and Qoboza and Klaaste were held without charge for months at Modderbee Prison, according to South African History Online.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: The bannings and detentions followed the September 1977 death in police custody of Black Consciousness Movement leader Steve Biko and accompanied the government's move to outlaw nineteen Black Consciousness organizations on the same day.
incidents.outcome_note: Qoboza was released from detention in March 1978 after international pressure, but The World did not resume publication.
